requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.

findings.claim: The change can break the build for users who already excluded their resolver. The generated partial resolver declaration now always carries `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, and the attribute has AllowMultiple=false. A user who already wrote `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on their own `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class` now gets error CS0579 (duplicate attribute). Those are exactly the users who care about coverage. This violates the derived criterion that generated code still compiles.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageUserAnnotatedResolverTests.UserAnnotatedResolver_StillCompiles. It passes on base and is expected to fail on head with CS0579 on MyResolver.

findings.claim: Every generated `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it can target classes there. So the guard drops the attribute for no reason. Any consumer project targeting net472 or netstandard2.0 (a common case for libraries whose coverage is measured) gets formatters and resolvers with no attribute. The acceptance criterion 'all generated code is decorated' is not met on those targets, and netstandard2.1 is treated differently from netstandard2.0.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageFrameworkSymbolTests.FormatterHasExcludeFromCodeCoverage with NETFRAMEWORK and with NETSTANDARD2_0. The test drives MessagePackGenerator with that preprocessor symbol defined and asserts that the generated MyObject formatter type carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. It fails on head because the #if strips the attribute.

findings.claim: the change's tests do not detect swap-boolean at src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/AnalyzerOptions.cs:206

receipt_plan.detail: public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; init; } = true; -> public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; init; } = false;

hunches.claim: Coverage exclusion is skipped for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework, so the requirement that all generated code carries the attribute is not met there. The templates wrap every attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. That guard is unnecessary: `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, and it can target classes. Projects on those targets, which includes most multi-targeted libraries, get no coverage exclusion. The README also says the attribute is not available on those targets, which is false. The derived criterion only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist.

receipt_plan.detail: Step 1: compile `[System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] class C {}` against `ReferenceAssemblies.NetStandard.NetStandard20` and against `ReferenceAssemblies.NetFramework.Net472.Default`; expect zero errors on both. Step 2: run MessagePackGenerator over a [MessagePackObject] type with `CSharpParseOptions.WithPreprocessorSymbols("NETSTANDARD2_0")`. Check the generated formatter's INamedTypeSymbol (and its containing types) for ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute; on head it is absent.

hunches.claim: The opt-out does not cover composite resolvers. CompositeResolverTemplate emits `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on the composite resolver and its FormatterCache<T> without checking `Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`. The README promises that `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false` opts out all generated formatters and resolvers, but generated composite resolvers stay excluded from coverage.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate from a source with `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false)] partial class R {}` plus `[CompositeResolver(typeof(R), typeof(MessagePack.Resolvers.StandardResolver))] partial class C {}`. Assert that no generated type symbol for C carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute; it fails on head.

hunches.claim: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard skips the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework builds, so generated code in those projects is still counted in coverage. The requirement says all generated code should be decorated. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists on net472 and netstandard2.0 in .NET Framework 4.0+, so the guard looks unnecessary and the outcome is inconsistent across TFMs. The guard is evaluated against the user's compilation symbols, so netstandard2.1 and net8 builds get the attribute while net472 builds do not.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile a generated formatter in a net472 or netstandard2.0 project, then use reflection or a coverage run to check whether the formatter carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. The attribute is absent despite being available.

hunches.claim: The CompositeResolverTemplate emits the attribute unconditionally, ignoring the new Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage setting, while every other template honors it. Setting ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false on the attribute therefore still leaves the composite resolver and its FormatterCache decorated, so the opt-out is inconsistent.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate with [GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false)] on a composite resolver and assert the output has no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage.

hunches.claim:
The TransformUtilities change from `{` to `{
` when nesting types have constraints alters whitespace in generated output for every nested generic-constrained type. This is unrelated to the requirement, and it matters because the new `#if` line follows the nesting brace. Without the newline `{#if` could be glued on the same line, but the change also modifies output for users who snapshot generated files.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests for nested types with generic constraints and check the diff in the generated files.

hunches.claim: CompositeResolverTemplate (.tt and .cs) emits ExcludeFromCodeCoverage unconditionally, ignoring the new Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage opt-out, unlike every other template. README says opt-out is via GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false), and this makes the opt-out incomplete for composite resolvers.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate a CompositeResolver (via the [CompositeResolver] attribute) with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false and assert the output has no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute; it will fail. Also CompositeResolverTemplate.cs does not read Options at all.

hunches.claim: The new test only asserts opt-out on a GeneratedMessagePackResolver and does not cover CompositeResolver output, so the unconditional emission is not caught. AllGeneratedTypes test also never exercises the composite resolver or generic formatters/nested types.

No test covers the opt-out for composite resolvers, so the inconsistency is undetected. The opt-out test only exercises GeneratedMessagePackResolver and never generates a composite resolver.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/CompositeResolverTemplate.cs:27 remove-guard: delete the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute emission -> expected to survive because TestSource has no CompositeResolver and only snapshot tests (withheld) cover it; and no test asserts opt-out on composite output

hunches.claim: The guard test counts guarded occurrences only for two exact string shapes, and the opt-out test only asserts the absence of the attribute text. No test compiles generated output under netstandard2.0/NETFRAMEWORK defines, so a wrong guard symbol (e.g. NETSTANDARD2_0 mistyped) would still pass because the test compares against the same constant Guard.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/FormatterTemplate.tt:14 swap guard symbol: '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' -> '#if !NETSTANDARD2_1'; the test would fail only if Guard constant is unchanged, so the real defect of the guard being semantically wrong on net472/netstandard2.0 consumers is not checked (no compile with those preprocessor symbols); survives if the constant is edited with the template

hunches.claim: The AnalyzerUtilities parsing `is not false` is only tested via explicit false and the default. The unset/default path is covered by the first test, but nothing tests that explicit `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = true` works, or that the option is honored for the other generator options flow (e.g., an assembly-level or multi-resolver case). Mutation swapping `is not false` to `is true` would be caught by the default test, but a mutation that ignores the argument entirely (`-> true`) is killed only by the opt-out test, which is OK; the nested-type brace change has no direct test.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/AnalyzerUtilities.cs:76 negate-condition: `is not false` -> `is not true`; expected to be killed by default test, confirm by running tests

hunches.claim: CompositeResolverTemplate emits `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on the composite resolver and its FormatterCache<T> unconditionally. Every other template checks `Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`. A user who sets `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false` on `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` still gets the attribute on generated composite resolvers, and no opt-out exists for them.

receipt_plan.detail: CompositeResolverTemplate.tt lines 7-9 and 35-37 have no `<# if (Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage) #>` guard. Compare ResolverTemplate.tt lines 14-18, which has the guard.

hunches.claim: The new public property `GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` is added to the runtime assembly's public API. Its default is true, which changes generated output for every existing user without opt-in. Users who check in or snapshot generated output, or who build with analyzers enabled, will see the diff. This is the purpose of the requirement, but the new public surface is optional per the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Public API additions in the 4 PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt files; the requirement states that a setting is optional.

hunches.claim: Generated code does not decorate every generated type. Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is read from the GeneratedMessagePackResolver attribute, so it controls only resolver-based generation. If formatters are generated through analyzer-only paths that have no GeneratedMessagePackResolver attribute, the option falls back to true, which is fine; but any attribute named argument parsing with `is not false` treats a non-bool value as true, so the setting is hard to disable.

receipt_plan.detail: Read AnalyzerUtilities.cs: GetSingleNamedArgumentValue(...) is not false defaults to true when the argument is missing or null.

hunches.claim: The attribute is skipped on netstandard2.0/.NET Framework, so the requirement 'all generated code is decorated' is not met on those targets, though the guard is needed to compile. README documents it; the acceptance criterion allows conditional emission.

narrative: This run reviews reading B of REQ-2297 on branch review/ju26-issue-2297/B: Opt-out setting, which the requirement explicitly calls acceptable: same template edits, plus a boolean on the generator options (e.g. read from an MSBuild/analyzer-config property or from the GeneratedMessagePackResolver attribute), default true. Each template wraps the attribute line in `<# if (Options.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage) { #> ... <# } #>`, so users who want coverage of generated code can disable it. As built on the branch: Make [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on generated code opt-out via GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false), default true; composite resolvers still always get it.
